title: Πόλεμος καὶ Ὕβρις
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 319. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Θεοὶ πάντες ἔγημαν ἣν ἕκαστος εἴληφεν ἐν κλήρῳ.
sentences.tr: Theoi pantes egēman hēn hekastos eilēphen en klērōi.
sentences.l: All the gods married the one whom each had received by lot.
sentences.n: The relative ἥν has no expressed antecedent and is feminine: 'the one (woman) whom'. ἐν κλήρῳ is 'in the allotment', the drawing of lots by which the gods regularly divide what is to be shared out. ἕκαστος, singular, stands inside a plural verb — Greek distributes freely between the group and its members.

sentences.t: Πόλεμος παρῆν ἐσχάτῳ κλήρῳ· Ὕβριν δὲ μόνην κατέλαβεν· ταύτης περισσῶς ἐρασθεὶς ἔγημεν.
sentences.tr: Polemos parēn eschatōi klērōi· Hybrin de monēn katelaben· tautēs perissōs erastheis egēmen.
sentences.l: War was present at the last lot; and Insolence alone he found; having fallen exceedingly in love with her, he married her.
sentences.i: War's turn came last of all, and he found only Insolence left; falling violently in love with her, he married her.
sentences.n: Both names are personified: Πόλεμος is masculine and Ὕβρις feminine, so the Greek gives the match its bride and bridegroom without saying a word about it. ὕβρις is wider than 'insolence' — the overbearing violence that treats others as there to be used. ἐράω takes the genitive of the person loved (ταύτης), and its aorist passive participle ἐρασθείς is active in sense, 'having fallen in love'.

sentences.l: And he follows after her as she walks everywhere.
sentences.i: And he follows at her heels wherever she goes.
sentences.n: The tense shifts to the present: the marriage was once, the following is always. ἐπακολουθέω takes the dative, and βαδιζούσῃ agrees with αὐτῇ.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἔνθα ⟨ἂν⟩ προέλθῃ ὕβρις ἢ ἐν πόλει ἢ ἐν ἔθνεσι, πόλεμος καὶ μάχαι εὐθὺς μετ’ αὐτὴν ἀκολουθεῖ.
sentences.tr: Hoti entha ⟨an⟩ proelthēi hybris ē en polei ē en ethnesi, polemos kai machai euthys met’ autēn akolouthei.
sentences.l: That where insolence ⟨may⟩ come forth, whether in a city or among nations, war and battles at once follow after her.
sentences.i: The story shows that wherever insolence comes forth, whether in a city or among whole nations, war and fighting follow straight after her.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. The angle brackets are Chambry's own supplement — he adds ἄν so that ἔνθα with the subjunctive προέλθῃ gives the indefinite 'wherever'. ἀκολουθεῖ is singular beside the double subject πόλεμος καὶ μάχαι, taking its number from the first member alone, though the plural μάχαι stands nearer to it; μετ’ αὐτήν, feminine, is Insolence herself.
